Parameter names of a fitted mvgam model

Source: R/index-mvgam.R
index-mvgam.Rd

variables() lists the name of every quantity in a fitted model's draws. hypothesis.mvgam(), as_draws(), as.data.frame.mvgam(), mcmc_plot.mvgam() and posterior_average.mvgam() accept these names. summary.mvgam() and posterior_summary() label their rows with them.

Usage

# S3 method for mvgam
variables(x, ...)

Arguments

x

A fitted mvgam object.

...

Unused. Anything passed here is refused.

Value

A character vector of parameter names.

How parameters are named

Observation parameters take their brms names, such as b_x, sds_sx_1, sd_site__Intercept and r_site[a,Intercept]. The trend model's parameters take the same names with a _trend suffix, such as b_x_trend or sds_sx_1_trend.

An index that runs over the series takes the series' name, as brms labels a grouping factor's levels. A model with series DM and DO has sigma_trend[DM], ar1_trend[DM] and the innovation covariance Sigma_trend[DM,DO]. A VAR's coefficients keep the lag as a number, as in Phi_trend[1,DM,DO], as do the changepoints of PW() in delta_trend[3,DM]. Factor loadings are Z_tilde[DM,1], with the factor as the second index. In a factor model the dynamics belong to the factors, as in ar1_trend[1]. The latent state matrices keep numeric indices, as in trend[12,1] for time 12 of the first series.

A bare name such as variable = "sigma_trend" selects every element of a vector, as in posterior. Because variables() includes the latent states, its output runs to hundreds of names on most fits. grep() narrows it, as in grep("^(sigma|ar1)_trend", variables(fit), value = TRUE).

See also

mvgam_draws to extract draws by name, hypothesis.mvgam() to test them, summary.mvgam() and posterior_summary() to summarise them.

Other posterior summaries: VarCorr.mvgam(), bibtex(), how_to_cite.mvgam(), hypothesis.mvgam(), mcmc_plot.mvgam(), methods_md(), mvgam_draws, pairs.mvgam(), posterior_interval.mvgam(), ranef.mvgam(), smooths.mvgam(), summary.mvgam()

Author

Nicholas J Clark

Examples

# \dontrun{
set.seed(13)
simdat <- sim_mvgam(n_series = 2L, trend_model = AR())
mod <- mvgam(y ~ x,
             trend_formula = ~ AR(),
             data = simdat$data_train,
             chains = 2, silent = 2)
#> Warning: 19 of 2000 (1.0%) transitions ended with a divergence.
#> See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings for details.
#> Warning: 2 of 2 chains had an E-BFMI less than 0.3.
#> See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings for details.

# The trend dynamics, indexed by series
grep("^(sigma|ar1)_trend", variables(mod), value = TRUE)
#> [1] "sigma_trend[series_1]" "sigma_trend[series_2]" "ar1_trend[series_1]"  
#> [4] "ar1_trend[series_2]"  

# Every element of a vector by its bare name
as_draws_df(mod, variable = "sigma_trend")
#> # A draws_df: 1000 iterations, 2 chains, and 2 variables
#>    sigma_trend[series_1] sigma_trend[series_2]
#> 1                   0.48                  0.42
#> 2                   0.38                  0.63
#> 3                   0.32                  0.71
#> 4                   0.41                  0.73
#> 5                   0.38                  0.60
#> 6                   0.31                  0.68
#> 7                   0.49                  0.87
#> 8                   0.36                  0.75
#> 9                   0.44                  0.82
#> 10                  0.56                  0.87
#> # ... with 1990 more draws
#> # ... hidden reserved variables {'.chain', '.iteration', '.draw'}

# Two series' autoregressive coefficients compared
hypothesis(mod, "ar1_trend[series_1] > ar1_trend[series_2]",
           class = NULL)
#> Hypothesis Tests for class :
#>                 Hypothesis Estimate Est.Error CI.Lower CI.Upper Evid.Ratio
#> 1 (ar1_trend[series... > 0    -0.21      0.42    -0.99     0.36       0.52
#>   Post.Prob Star
#> 1      0.34     
#> ---
#> 'CI': 90%-CI for one-sided and 95%-CI for two-sided hypotheses.
#> '*': For one-sided hypotheses, the posterior probability exceeds 95%;
#> for two-sided hypotheses, the value tested against lies outside the 95%-CI.
#> Posterior probabilities of point hypotheses assume equal prior probabilities.

# Next, plot chosen parameters with mcmc_plot(mod, variable = ...)
# }
